title: What is uṣūl for?
summary: Understand the book’s purpose, its four parts, and why Ibn Rushd distinguishes the examination of sound inference from even universal practical knowledge.
prerequisites: No previous study of uṣūl is required. Begin with the difference between knowing what to do and knowing how a conclusion is justified.

terms.definition: The discipline examining legal rulings, their sources, the means of deriving them, and the qualifications of the jurist; Ibn Rushd gives the third task special prominence.
Knowledge of legal rulings concerning acts, such as prayer and almsgiving.
Assent or conviction: the end of the first kind of knowledge in §2, namely a judgement formed in the soul, distinct from a practical act.
A disciplined art or craft possessing methods and rules; it does not mean merely a manual occupation here.
Induction: in §4, validating many universal notions through the examination of early legal opinions case by case—not claiming that every methodological principle was first discovered in this way.
A rule that guides inquiry and helps protect the mind against error.
Method of examination or investigation in §2. The original instrument image is explained by Ibn Rushd’s comparison with a compass and straightedge; ‘probe’ is too literal as the main translation.
Practitioners of kalām (dialectical theology), not generic discussants. In §§7 and 9 Ibn Rushd refers to their treatment of uṣūl and logical questions; §11 invokes their technical usage.

basic.objective: Explain why a jurist needs rules of inquiry as well as knowledge of particular rulings.
explanation: In §1 Ibn Rushd describes a concise reminder drawn from al-Ghazālī’s al-Mustaṣfā. Its brevity does not make it an elementary textbook. The guide therefore begins with the orientation that §8 says a learner needs: the discipline’s purpose, place among the sciences, name and divisions.

Section 2 distinguishes knowledge directed towards assent (iʿtiqād), knowledge directed towards action, and knowledge of the rules that regulate inquiry. Knowledge of universal rulings or legal sources is still practical rather than automatically methodological. Sections 3–4 explain why later jurists need rules stated explicitly, although earlier jurists could exercise the relevant capacity without a separate formal discipline. Section 5 maps four inquiries: rulings, sources, derivation and the jurist.

example.title: A ruler for thought
example.text: Section 2 compares rules of inquiry with a compass and straightedge. Knowing a particular prayer ruling resembles possessing an answer; knowing how evidence supports that ruling concerns the method used to reach it.

tasks: Which of the four parts in §5 examines how a ruling is derived?
Does §4 say the Companions lacked the relevant reasoning capacity? Explain.
feedback: The third part examines proofs and their use in deriving rulings from sources. The fourth examines who possesses the required competence.
No. Ibn Rushd explicitly distinguishes exercising a capacity from formally studying its rules. Their opinions can themselves supply material from which later thinkers identify universal principles.

intermediate.objective: Reconstruct the relation between Ibn Rushd’s preferred scientific arrangement and the arrangement he actually follows.
explanation: Section 6 identifies the third part as the discipline’s distinctive inquiry because it supplies methods of derivation; the other parts concern knowledge directed towards action. The phrase min tilka (‘of those’) refers back most naturally to those other parts when Ibn Rushd introduces two approaches to their disputed premises. Yet §7 retains al-Ghazālī’s fourfold arrangement and refers expressly to the practice of the mutakallimūn, practitioners of kalām. Distinguish a strict classification of the science from this book’s pedagogical organization.

Ibn Rushd contrasts accepting widely recognized methodological premises with explaining how derivation proceeds under different opinions, such as those of the Ẓāhirīs and defenders of qiyās. He prefers the comparative treatment as more useful, without treating all opinions as equally correct. Section 148 returns to the distinctive inquiry: understanding prophetic meaning through wording and indications. Section 9 omits a logical introduction on grounds of disciplinary placement, not opposition to logic; al-Ghazālī himself described his logical prologue as a general introduction to sciences rather than a constituent part of uṣūl.

example.title: Different starting commitments
example.text: In §6 Ibn Rushd proposes explaining derivation both for the Ẓāhirīs and for proponents of qiyās. The methodological task includes showing what follows from each position; the passage does not declare the positions identical.

tasks: Why does retaining four parts in §7 not refute the classification in §6?
What additional work does the comparative option in §6 require?
feedback: The classification identifies the discipline’s distinctive function; the adopted arrangement also accommodates established teaching practice. Both claims can hold together.
It requires stating disputed principles and showing the rules and consequences of deriving rulings under each. Listing rival conclusions alone would not complete that task.

advanced.objective: Formulate a defensible account of the relation between implicit practice, induction and explicit methodological rules.
explanation: Read §§2–4 as a connected argument: classificatory ends of knowledge, the historical need for articulated standards, and early legal opinions as materials for verifying general methodological notions. The wording of §4 says that many such notions were validated (ṣuḥḥiḥat) through induction, not that every principle of uṣūl was originally discovered from Companion fatwās or that every fatwā is beyond criticism.

A comparison with logical works and al-Mustaṣfā must test the exact arguments and their disciplinary setting. Ibn Rushd’s reference to the mutakallimūn in §§7 and 9 identifies theologians active in uṣūl, not everyone discussing the field. The compass analogy alone does not establish identity with demonstrative syllogistic; omitting a logical prolegomenon in §9 does not establish hostility to logic. Al-Ghazālī also describes his prologue as a general preliminary, not part of uṣūl proper.

example.title: An objection answered by practice
example.text: The objection in §4 points to the earliest generation’s lack of formal investigation. Ibn Rushd answers by distinguishing implicit competence from explicit study and by referring to their legal opinions as evidence.

tasks: Reconstruct that reply in three steps, preserving the limited scope of the induction claim.
Design one source comparison that could test whether §6’s comparative method is already present in al-Mustaṣfā.
feedback: A sound reconstruction identifies the objection, implicit practical competence, and the inductive verification of many—not all—general notions. It must not turn the Companions' prior judgements into proof that every inherited opinion is correct.

Research criteria: locate an exact parallel, compare the proposed treatment of rival principles, and record agreement and divergence. A thematic resemblance or shared vocabulary is a lead, not a completed demonstration of dependence.

title: How does a ruling concern an act?
summary: Distinguish the legal ruling, its source of authority, the person addressed and the act concerned before studying its subdivisions.
prerequisites: Know the four-part map in lesson 1. No detailed knowledge of the five rulings is assumed.

terms.definition: A legal ruling concerning an act; its definition and elements are examined separately in §§10–11 and §36.
Address or discourse; in this discussion, the Law’s address to a legally responsible person.
A person to whom a legally binding demand can be directed, subject to the conditions later examined.
Permitted: an act for which the Law indicates equality between doing and omitting it.
Obligatory: in §17, an act preferred by the Law’s address with a threat attached to its unqualified omission.

basic.objective: Identify the five classifications and distinguish a ruling from the person and act to which it relates.
explanation: Section 10 announces four questions about rulings: definition, divisions, constituent elements and what manifests them. Section 11 begins with the definition attributed to the People of the Sunna. It also reports a disagreement about goodness and badness; keep the speakers distinct as you read.

Section 17 provides the essential map. A demand to act may be obligatory or recommended; a demand to omit may be prohibitive or disapproving; permission allows either. Section 36 then distinguishes the one who rules, the person subject to the ruling, and the matter ruled upon. These are different questions about the same legal relation.

example.title: Prayer as act and ruling
example.text: Using the book’s recurring prayer example, separate performing the prayer, the person addressed, and the legal demand concerning performance. Naming the act does not itself explain the character or conditions of that demand.

tasks: What distinguishes an obligatory act from a recommended act in §17?
Is the person subject to a ruling the same element as the act ruled upon?
feedback: Both involve a preference for performance. The definition of obligation includes a threat for unqualified omission; recommendation lacks that feature.
No. Section 36 separates them. Later questions about a person’s understanding concern the addressee, while questions about an act’s possibility concern the act.

intermediate.objective: Explain how definitions, attribution and technical conventions prevent misleading summaries of the ruling discussion.
explanation: Section 11 reports positions of the People of the Sunna and the Muʿtazilites concerning the status of goodness and badness. Section 13 says that neither argument presented suffices to settle the question and places the issue outside the current discipline. A summary must therefore preserve more than the first reported definition.

Section 17 also separates a difference in terminology from a difference in meaning: Abū Ḥanīfa’s followers use farḍ and wājib according to the certainty of the supporting judgement. Section 37 distinguishes divine ruling authority from the obedience owed to human authorities by virtue of that authority.

example.title: Two names for different evidential grades
example.text: In §17 the distinction between farḍ and wājib tracks whether the relevant threat is established certainly or probably. Ibn Rushd’s response requires understanding the intended distinction before disputing the names.

tasks: Why is ‘Ibn Rushd proves all goodness is relational in §11’ an inadequate summary?
Does §17’s comment about names show that certainty and probability are interchangeable?
feedback: It erases the attribution of arguments and §13’s judgement that the presented arguments do not settle the issue. Reported doctrine and the author’s evaluation must be separated.
No. The evidential distinction remains intelligible. His comment addresses the use of labels once meanings have been understood; it does not erase the difference those labels mark.

advanced.objective: Assess how theological premises enter a discipline that repeatedly limits its treatment of theology.
explanation: Compare §6’s two ways of handling disputed principles with the procedure in §§11–17. Ibn Rushd reports doctrinal commitments, considers arguments and at points identifies consequences relevant to legal reasoning. He also declines to resolve every theological dispute within uṣūl. The boundary concerns the task and treatment of a question, rather than the absence of all theological assumptions.

Section 12 distinguishes widespread agreement from rational necessity. Section 16 differentiates positions about acts before revelation. A research account should explain why these distinctions matter without treating every reported position as Ibn Rushd’s own final doctrine.

example.title: Agreement is not necessity
example.text: Section 12 addresses the argument from rational persons’ agreement about truthfulness and lying. Ibn Rushd denies that being widely accepted, by itself, establishes that a proposition is rationally necessary.

tasks: Identify what §12’s criticism establishes and what it leaves undecided.
Propose a precise comparison with al-Mustaṣfā concerning the placement and use of the goodness/badness dispute.
feedback: It rejects a particular inference from acceptance to necessity. It does not by itself prove the opposite moral theory or dispose of every argument for intrinsic goodness.

Research criteria: compare the exact argument, its attribution, and its stated relevance to analogy or juristic error. Establish what is retained, altered or bracketed before making a claim about Ibn Rushd’s overall position.

title: What counts as obligation?
summary: Follow the difference between an obligatory end, permitted alternatives, an extended time and the means needed to perform the act.
prerequisites: Distinguish obligation, recommendation and permission using §17 or lesson 2.

terms.definition: An obligation allowing a choice among a specified set of alternative acts.
An obligation whose performance is permitted within an extended period rather than at one fixed instant.
A condition; §23 distinguishes a condition of being obliged from an obtainable means needed to perform the duty.
Probable judgement; §25 uses a judgement about likely survival to evaluate permitted postponement.

basic.objective: Explain why a duty can allow a choice of act or time while remaining a duty.
explanation: Section 18 distinguishes a determinate obligation from an obligation allowing specified alternatives, and from an obligation with an extended time. Choosing one permitted way of fulfilling a duty differs from being free to abandon the duty altogether. Section 20 points to expiation alternatives and prayer periods as legal examples.

Sections 21–22 explain the apparent puzzle of an early prayer: a person may delay it, yet performing it discharges the obligation. The permission to postpone is qualified by a resolve to perform. Section 23 adds another distinction: an obtainable means, such as ritual purity for prayer, can be obligatory for the sake of the required act.

example.title: Praying early in an allowed period
example.text: In §§21–22, prayer at the beginning of its period discharges the duty even though omission at that particular moment can be allowed. Permission to choose the time does not amount to permission to omit prayer entirely.

tasks: Why does an extended period not turn the whole duty into a mere recommendation?
Why does §23 treat ritual purity differently from the capacity to walk?
feedback: The duty still has to be discharged. Section 22 distinguishes permitted postponement with a resolve to act from resolving to abandon the act altogether.
Ritual purity is presented as obtainable by choice for the duty’s sake. The capacity to walk is a condition of imposing a duty, not itself something commanded into existence.

intermediate.objective: Separate disputes about the definition of obligation from disputes about the conditions governing postponement.
explanation: Sections 19–20 distinguish a metaphysical objection to alternatives from the legal evidence that such obligations occur. Sections 21–22 then address a more specific definitional objection: how can an act be obligatory now if omission now incurs no punishment? The response uses different respects and the continuing resolve to perform.

Section 25 introduces prospective judgement. A later death does not automatically show that an earlier permitted delay was disobedience. What matters is the judgement about survival under which the delay was allowed. The reported disagreement over postponing pilgrimage concerns that judgement; it is not simply a dispute over the dictionary meaning of ‘command’.

example.title: Unexpected death within the period
example.text: Section 25 considers a person who dies during the allotted period before performing the duty. Ibn Rushd rejects an automatic inference of disobedience and discusses the probability under which postponement was permissible.

tasks: Distinguish permission to postpone from a prediction guaranteed to come true.
What does the expiation example establish in §20, and what broader issue does Ibn Rushd set aside?
feedback: Permitted postponement depends on a justified expectation and the resolve to perform; subsequent events can defeat that expectation without retrospectively proving an intention to abandon the duty.
The example establishes the occurrence of alternatives in the Law. It does not settle the whole metaphysics of possibility, foreknowledge and human choice, which Ibn Rushd says belongs elsewhere.

advanced.objective: Test whether the obligation discussion supplies one uniform rule or several rules with different conditions.
explanation: Reconstruct three distinct problems: the object demanded, the time allowed, and the conditions needed for performance. Section 23’s account of necessary means distinguishes what the agent can acquire from what conditions the possibility of an obligation. Its minimum-performance discussion adds a further qualification concerning acts whose parts occur successively.

Compare §§21–25 with §201, where timing is not determined by the imperative form alone. The Bidāya application B16 is a useful control: it reports that the pilgrimage dispute involves the structure of available periods and the risk of death, beyond a simple immediacy/delay formula. Treat the card as a located parallel to investigate.

example.title: How much performance is sufficient?
example.text: Section 23 uses wiping the head and remaining still in bowing when discussing the minimum to which a name applies. Application B02 shows why the corresponding fiqh dispute also requires grammatical and transmitted evidence.

tasks: State the qualifications needed before applying ‘a necessary means is obligatory’ here.
Explain why §23 alone cannot establish every school’s ruling about how much of the head must be wiped.
feedback: Identify an established duty, a genuinely necessary means, and the agent’s ability to acquire it. Do not convert every condition of capacity into a new commanded act.

The passage gives a methodological distinction. Establishing the legally relevant act and its extent requires further evidence. Research should test the verse, reported practice and competing meanings rather than read a complete ruling out of a slogan.

title: Can an act be both commanded and forbidden?
summary: Distinguish the respect under which an act is judged, the force of prohibitive wording, and whether the act has legal effect.
prerequisites: Know the five rulings. Keep the question ‘Is this forbidden?’ separate from ‘Does this discharge a duty or produce a legal effect?’

terms.definition: A contrary; §28 tests incompatibility in the same thing, at the same time and in the same respect.
Prohibition or prohibitive address; the force of its wording is examined separately from the act’s legal effect.
An accompanying indication that can affect how an expression is understood.
Validity; its precise meaning depends on the context and terminology identified in §56.
Disapproval, distinguished here from strict forbiddance when interpreting a prohibition.

basic.objective: Explain why different descriptions of one act must be distinguished before claiming a contradiction.
explanation: Section 28 begins with a logical condition: opposite rulings cannot attach to one act at one time in the same respect. Different times, acts or respects must be distinguished. This prepares the legal question whether a prohibited circumstance invalidates an otherwise required performance.

Section 31 considers prayer on usurped land. Ibn Rushd distinguishes the respect in which the movements are prayer from the respect in which they occupy another person’s land. His point requires attention to both descriptions. Section 56 helps distinguish legal validity from the separate question of whether conduct was blameworthy.

example.title: Prayer and wrongful occupation
example.text: In §31 the same movements are described as commanded prayer and as prohibited occupation in different respects. Ibn Rushd rejects an argument that treats this combination as a contradiction simply because the physical movements are identical.

tasks: Name the two respects in the usurped-land example.
Does recognizing different respects mean that the wrongful occupation becomes permitted?
feedback: One concerns the performance of prayer; the other concerns occupying land without right. The identity of the bodily movement does not erase that distinction.

No. Separating the descriptions allows the wrong to remain wrong while its relation to the prayer’s validity is examined. Validity is not a general declaration that every associated act is permissible.

intermediate.objective: Follow the transition from the logic of contrary rulings to the interpretation of a qualified prohibition.
explanation: Section 28 reports differing accounts of an external cause and an attribute attached to the act. Section 29 then distinguishes inquiry into the verbal form of prohibition from inquiry into its established meaning. An earlier unqualified command may supply an indication for construing a later prohibition as disapproval.

Once a genuinely prohibitive meaning concerning an act under a qualification is established, Ibn Rushd says the act is invalidated insofar as it bears that qualification. Section 206 returns to this position within the discussion of expressions. Section 30’s objection to placement matters: the problem partly belongs to interpreting evidence, not simply listing rulings.

example.title: A prohibited place of prayer
example.text: Section 31 says that someone who permits prayer in the listed places should explain how the relevant prohibition is understood. The example connects a conclusion about validity to an interpretation of the prohibitive address.

tasks: Why is ‘every sentence in prohibitive form automatically invalidates the act’ too quick?
How does §30 help explain the return to this question in §206?
feedback: The force of the expression must first be established. Section 29 considers indications that can shift apparent forbiddance towards disapproval; the conclusion cannot bypass that interpretive step.
Ibn Rushd thinks the issue involves how wording signifies. Its later placement among commands and prohibitions supplies the methodological setting missing from a bare classification of rulings.

advanced.objective: Assess the apparent tension between different-respect analysis and invalidation through a prohibited qualification.
explanation: Do not dissolve the tension between §31 and §§29,206 by selecting one sentence. First determine whether the prohibited matter is being treated as another respect of the act, a qualification entering the relevant legal description, or an expression whose force has been redirected. Then identify what ‘invalidity’ means in the context.

Applications B03 and B18 offer concrete comparisons involving a forbidden preliminary act and a forbidden divorce. Their descriptions identify illustrative parallels, not explicit cross-citations. A research account must compare the actual reasoning and relevant reports before treating either case as a direct execution of one universal formula.

example.title: Menstrual divorce as a control case
example.text: Section 28 reports al-Shāfiʿī’s giving effect to divorce during menstruation while locating its prohibition in the infliction of harm. Application B18 supplies an applied comparison involving validity, proper performance and the relevant report.

tasks: What must a proposed reconciliation of §§29,31,206 explain?
What evidence would distinguish an interpretive disagreement from a merely terminological disagreement in a Bidāya case?
feedback: It must preserve the separate-respect argument, the prior determination of prohibitive force, and the limited phrase ‘insofar as’ the act bears the qualification. Treat unexplained tensions as questions for further work.

Research criteria: identify each party’s account of the prohibition, the relevant condition and the resulting legal effect. Shared use of ‘valid’ or ‘invalid’ does not establish that they mean or infer the same thing.

title: Who can be addressed?
summary: Distinguish understanding, a legal sign of maturity, capacity for action and legal consequences affecting someone who is not directly responsible.
prerequisites: Distinguish the person addressed from the act concerned using §36 or lesson 2.

terms.definition: The imposition of a legally binding demand upon a person, subject to conditions of understanding and capacity.
Puberty, treated in §42 as a legally appointed sign because the development of reason is difficult to determine individually.
Reason or understanding; here relevant to comprehending the Law’s address.
Capacity to act; §45 rejects imposing what lies beyond capacity.
A guardian, who may be the person addressed concerning obligations connected with a child or the child’s property.

basic.objective: Explain why absence of direct responsibility does not remove every legal consequence connected with a child.
explanation: Section 38 says that an obligatory address presupposes understanding it. The objection about children’s property then reveals an important distinction: a legal matter can concern a child while the guardian is the person commanded to act. Similarly, the command to require a child’s prayer is directed to the father.

Section 42 identifies puberty as a condition known through the Law. It is an appointed sign, because the acquisition of reason varies and is difficult to determine separately in every individual. Section 45 adds the requirement of capacity: a demand cannot simply require an impossible act.

example.title: A child’s property
example.text: When §38 considers alms and financial liabilities connected with children, it directs attention to the guardian. The child’s lack of direct moral responsibility does not itself answer every question about the property.

tasks: Who is the addressee in §38’s response about a child’s property?
Does §42 claim that the physical event of puberty instantly creates reason?
feedback: The guardian is the legally responsible addressee in the response. Distinguish that person from the child or property to which the legal consequence relates.
No. The passage explicitly raises that difficulty. Puberty functions as a generally indicative legal sign where individual intellectual development is difficult to establish precisely.

intermediate.objective: Reconstruct how the text distinguishes a rational condition, a legal sign and an apparently troublesome counterexample.
explanation: Sections 38 and 42 give different accounts of two conditions: understanding the address is apprehended by reason, whereas puberty is a condition apprehended through the Law. The second can function as a practical sign without being the physical cause of the first.

The intoxication discussion tests the first condition. Section 38 distinguishes effective divorce according to those who recognize it from straightforward proof that an unintelligent addressee understands a command. Sections 39–40 offer readings of the verse, including an address to sober persons concerning later conduct. Section 41 leaves a broader theological problem to its own discipline.

example.title: An address before the relevant condition occurs
example.text: Section 40 considers the possibility that the prohibition relating to intoxication was addressed to hearers while sober. The time of receiving an intelligible address and the later condition regulated by it need not coincide.

tasks: Why does a divorce’s legal effectiveness not by itself prove full contemporaneous understanding?
How does the sober-addressee interpretation respond to the apparent difficulty?
feedback: Section 38 treats effectiveness, where accepted, as a separate legal consequence connected with earlier voluntary conduct. A legal effect cannot simply be equated with present comprehension.

It preserves an intelligible address to someone able to understand it while regulating a later situation. Its adequacy must still be evaluated as an interpretation of the passage, not assumed from logical possibility alone.

advanced.objective: Distinguish moral address, legal effects and institutional administration without reducing them to one notion of agency.
explanation: Build a map of three questions: who can understand a demand, what marks the condition legally, and which consequences follow from an act or state. Section 55’s account of appointed signs helps clarify §42, but does not authorize treating every legal consequence as punishment for a responsible choice.

The distinction between error and sin in §243 and the qualifications in §244 provide a further comparison. Application B26 concerns compensation after a physician’s mistake; B04 concerns zakāt on a child’s property. Both require identifying the type of legal consequence before inferring personal culpability. Their differing contexts must remain visible.

example.title: A financial claim and personal blame
example.text: Section 38 answers the objection about children’s alms and financial liabilities by identifying the guardian as addressee. Application B04 develops the related dispute over whether a minor’s zakāt is primarily worship or a financial right in wealth.

tasks: What inference does the distinction between compensation and sin block?
What would a rigorous comparison of §42 with a modern capacity rule require?
feedback: A financial consequence does not, merely by existing, establish a blameworthy act by its bearer. One must identify its legal ground and the person addressed.

Research criteria: compare the function of the sign, its authority, its relation to individual capacity and the consequence it triggers. Do not claim historical identity from a shared age threshold or a general concern with administrability.

title: What changes under coercion?
summary: Distinguish the possibility of choosing, the intention of obedience, the degree of pressure and the legal effect of an act.
prerequisites: Distinguish the act’s physical possibility, the person’s understanding and the act’s legal classification.

terms.definition: Coercion or pressure to act; §47 treats its means and severity as variable.
Choice: the ability to do otherwise, whose significance must be assessed alongside the pressure imposed.
Acquisition of an act by the agent; §§43–45 examine its relation to choice and capacity.
Obedience; §47 distinguishes doing an act under pressure from undertaking it with an understanding that it is obedience.
Independent juristic inquiry; the comparison of particular coercive harms in §47 is assigned to this kind of assessment.

basic.objective: Explain why coercion does not answer every question about choice, intention, reward and legal effect at once.
explanation: Sections 43–44 introduce the act as something the person can acquire by choice and connect devotional compliance with belief in the command. Section 47 then asks what pressure changes. A person may still be physically able to refuse, but the severity of what refusal would bring matters.

The passage first discusses pressure towards compliance. It distinguishes the initial motive for acting from the person’s understanding of the act when undertaking it. It then discusses pressure towards violation and separates two questions: blame for yielding and the assessment of resistance. Ibn Rushd treats the degrees and comparison of harms as matters requiring legal inquiry.

example.title: Pressure to perform a duty
example.text: Section 47 says that pressure may initially move a person to act, while at performance the person also understands the act as obedience. The passage therefore does not infer absence of devotional intention merely from the presence of pressure.

tasks: Can an initial external motive and a later intention of obedience coexist in this account?
Does the possibility of refusing settle whether the person is legally coerced in every respect?
feedback: Yes. Section 47 expressly allows this sequence when discussing reward for compliance. Identify the time at which the relevant intention is present.
No. The degree of threatened harm and the act demanded remain relevant. Physical alternatives alone do not complete the legal assessment.

intermediate.objective: Separate the account of willing an act from the legal judgement about acting under pressure.
explanation: Section 44 rejects an infinite sequence of wills required to will. It explains desire in relation to assent involving hope and fear, while continuing to distinguish an act acquired by the person from an occurrence outside that person’s control. Section 45 insists on meaningful human capacity.

Section 47 must be read with those distinctions rather than reduced to ‘the agent moved, therefore the act was fully free’. Its final comparison of coercive harm with the prohibited act is explicitly a question for ijtihād. Application B06 further distinguishes choosing to utter words from the legal freedom required for an effective divorce.

example.title: Choosing words under a threat
example.text: Application B06 reports disagreement over coerced divorce. The speaker may intentionally pronounce the words while the Law’s classification of coercion and the utterance’s legal effect remain disputed.

tasks: List three questions that remain distinct in the coerced-utterance example.
Why cannot the last part of §47 supply one automatic result for every threat?
feedback: Ask whether the words were intentionally spoken, whether the circumstances count as legal coercion, and whether the utterance produces its normal legal effect. Answers to one do not mechanically settle the others.
The text makes severity, the means of coercion and the kind of demanded act relevant. Comparing these is part of juristic inquiry; the passage does not give an exhaustive universal verdict.

advanced.objective: Evaluate the relationship between the text’s account of agency and its treatment of legal coercion, preserving unresolved cases.
explanation: The agency discussion and the coercion discussion operate at connected but different levels. Sections 44–45 defend the intelligibility of choice and capacity; §47 asks how particular pressures affect reward, blame and the evaluation of resistance. It does not infer that every physically available alternative is legally required.

Section 53 offers a useful comparison: hard cases involving unavoidable injury do not, for Ibn Rushd, overthrow the general principle about impossible demands. He presents more than one possible analysis. An advanced reading should preserve this openness and distinguish a principle of capacity from a fully adjudicated rule for each emergency.

example.title: Leaving a damaged field
example.text: In §53 a person in a usurped cultivated field causes injury whether remaining or leaving. Ibn Rushd considers reducing harm and other analyses; he does not present the predicament as proof that contradictory demands are straightforwardly imposed.

tasks: What would have to be established before moving from ‘could resist’ to ‘was obliged to resist’?
Design a comparison of §47 with the Bidāya discussion located in B06.
feedback: Identify the demanded act, the severity and kind of threatened harm, the relevant legal evidence and any ranking of competing claims. Bare physical possibility is insufficient.

Research criteria: track how each passage uses choice, coercion and legal effect; compare its examples and qualifications. Record any difference without claiming that the brief theoretical passage already resolves the entire applied dispute.

title: Do conditions cause rulings?
summary: Distinguish an obtainable legal condition, a condition of physical possibility and a sign through which a ruling is known to obtain.
prerequisites: Review lesson 3’s distinction between an obligatory act and an obtainable means needed for it.

terms.definition: A legal condition; §§49–50 discuss one that an agent can acquire, such as ritual purity for prayer.
A condition of actual existence or possibility, distinguished from an obtainable legal condition.
A cause or occasion; §§54–55 discuss causes that manifest legal rulings, with their force appointed by the Law.
A sign through which it is known that a ruling obtains.

basic.objective: Explain why failing to obtain a possible legal condition does not automatically remove the obligation to act.
explanation: Sections 49–50 ask whether a command can apply before a condition has been fulfilled. Ibn Rushd’s example is prayer before ritual purity has been acquired. Where the person can acquire the condition, the command concerns performing the act with that condition fulfilled. It does not command a valid prayer without its required purity.

Section 50 distinguishes this from lacking a condition of actual possibility. Section 55 introduces another relation: signs appointed by the Law through which rulings are known to obtain. Its comparison with perceptible causes explains a reliable connection; it does not make every legal condition a physical cause.

example.title: Prayer before ablution
example.text: In §49, someone cannot remove the duty to pray merely by never performing ablution. The relevant condition is within the person’s capacity, and the command concerns prayer performed after that condition is fulfilled.

tasks: Does this argument require performing a valid prayer while still ritually impure?
What must be checked before extending the argument to a different missing condition?
feedback: No. The command is understood on the supposition that the obtainable condition is fulfilled. It includes the required ordered performance.
Check whether the agent can acquire the condition and whether it is a legal condition of the act or a condition of actual possibility. The argument cannot erase genuine incapacity.

intermediate.objective: Reconstruct the equivocation identified in §50 and distinguish a condition’s existence from evidence of it.
explanation: The objection in §50 treats an act lacking its legal condition as impossible in the same sense as an act lacking a condition of actual existence. Ibn Rushd answers that the condition under discussion can be acquired. The whole ordered performance is therefore possible even though the legally complete act is not yet present.

Sections 42 and 55 add a different issue: a legally appointed sign can identify when a condition is treated as obtaining. Application B07 distinguishes actual financial maturity from a formal declaration releasing a ward. Read it as an illustration of a particular institutional dispute, not a claim that every judicial declaration is merely informational.

example.title: A condition and its appointed sign
example.text: Section 42 separates the acquisition of reason from puberty, the sign appointed because individual development is difficult to determine. Application B07 offers a further comparison involving actual maturity and a formal declaration concerning a ward.

tasks: State the two senses of ‘cannot occur’ that §50 distinguishes.
Why must a comparison with B07 establish what the official declaration does?
feedback: An act may lack a presently unfulfilled legal condition that can be obtained, or lack a condition making its occurrence possible at all. The objection treats these alike.
A declaration might establish a fact, alter a status or perform both functions. One cannot infer its legal role merely from calling it a sign or from observing that maturity exists independently.

advanced.objective: Clarify what the analogy with perceptible causes does and does not establish about legal explanation.
explanation: Section 55 speaks of appointed signs that entail the occurrence of rulings as perceptible causes entail effects. Attend both to the comparison and to the appointment by the Law. The passage concerns how rulings are manifested and known; it explicitly postpones the detailed conditions to Part III.

A rigorous analysis should distinguish the ontological condition of an act, the legal condition of its acceptability, a sign of responsibility, and the means by which an authority recognizes a relevant state. The text supplies examples for these distinctions, but does not present a single exhaustive taxonomy in this paragraph.

example.title: Puberty as an appointed indication
example.text: Section 42 explains that puberty does not suddenly add reason. It is appointed as a generally indicative sign because the individual emergence of reason is difficult to determine. This controls an overly physical reading of legal causation.

tasks: What inference from the cause analogy would §42 make doubtful?
Draft a source-based account of the relation among §§23,49–50 and §55.
feedback: It would be doubtful to infer that a legal sign must physically produce the capacity or state it indicates. Section 42 expressly distinguishes the sign from the development of reason.

Assessment criteria: distinguish obtainable means, conditions of possibility and appointed signs; explain the role of each example; preserve §55’s postponement of further analysis. Mark any claim about a comprehensive theory of causation as an interpretation requiring additional textual support.

title: Must an act be repeated?
summary: Separate validity, sufficient performance, repetition after a defect and a later duty to make up an observance.
prerequisites: Distinguish the original command from the conditions under which the act fulfils it.

terms.definition: Validity; §56 records different technical usages in worship and then treats contracts separately.
Sufficiency: performance that discharges the relevant duty when its prescribed character and conditions are fulfilled.
Timely performance of an obligation within its appointed period.
Repetition after an initial performance affected by a defect.
Make-up performance; §57 distinguishes several uses and warns against drawing the same inference from all of them.

basic.objective: Classify timely performance, repetition and make-up performance without inferring blame from the label alone.
explanation: Section 57 distinguishes performing within the allotted time, performing again after a defect, and performing after the time has elapsed. It also says that make-up terminology has several uses. A missed act caused by inadvertence differs in culpability from one deliberately omitted, even where the later performance receives the same name.

Section 56 records different meanings of validity in worship. Section 205 gives the crucial qualification for sufficient performance: the act must be complete, possess its prescribed character and meet all its conditions. Section 51 explains that a later duty to make up an act requires its own legal warrant.

example.title: Making up a fast after menstruation
example.text: Section 57 rejects the inference that a later obligation to make up fasting proves an earlier obligation to fast during menstruation. A later duty and an earlier duty are different claims.

tasks: Does every duty to make up an act prove blame for not performing it earlier?
Why does merely doing something commanded fail to establish sufficiency in §205?
feedback: No. The menstruation example and the distinction involving inadvertence show why the original duty, the later duty and blame must each be established.
The prescribed character and conditions matter. A command to complete an already defective pilgrimage does not make that defective performance sufficient to discharge every duty connected with it.

intermediate.objective: Explain the difference between a disagreement over validity terminology and a substantive claim about a renewed command.
explanation: Section 56 contrasts theologians’ usage of validity as conformity with the Law with jurists’ usage emphasizing sufficiency and removal of make-up liability. Its example of a person who believed himself ritually pure shows why the same word can answer different questions. Identify the convention before declaring a doctrinal contradiction.

Section 204 then examines the scope of a timed command. For the account Ibn Rushd presents as carefully distinguishing the issues, specifying time can be a condition of the commanded act, so an obligation after that time needs further evidence. Section 205 concerns a separate question: whether complete compliance suffices.

example.title: An invalidated pilgrimage must still be completed
example.text: Section 205 uses the command to complete an invalidated pilgrimage as an objection to automatic sufficiency. Ibn Rushd answers by qualifying complete compliance: a defect can prevent the performance from satisfying the original duty.

tasks: Separate the question asked in §204 from the question asked in §205.
Why is ‘the act was valid, therefore no later duty can arise’ not safe without further clarification?
feedback: Section 204 asks whether a timed command itself requires later make-up performance. Section 205 asks when performing a commanded act sufficiently discharges a duty.
One must identify the usage of ‘valid’ and whether a further command applies. Section 56 explicitly reports a usage compatible with make-up performance being required by renewed command.

advanced.objective: Evaluate inferences from performance and later liability while keeping the scope of each command explicit.
explanation: Map each example by original addressee, act, time, conditions and further legal address. This exposes several invalid shortcuts: later make-up does not prove an earlier duty; a command to complete an undertaking does not prove an initial duty to begin it; and a technically valid performance need not settle every later obligation.

Section 59 supplies another control. A person’s expectation of death does not itself cause the allotted period to expire. Probable judgement can affect the assessment of postponement without changing the objective time condition. Application B17 offers a related, explicitly illustrative distinction between beginning and completing ʿumra.

example.title: Expected death and an unexpired period
example.text: Section 59 rejects calling later performance ‘make-up’ merely because someone had expected to die earlier. When the expectation proves false, the prescribed time has not thereby elapsed.

tasks: Why does §59 matter for distinguishing culpability from the classification of performance?
What evidence is needed to extend §204’s argument to a particular missed observance?
feedback: The expectation may affect whether delay was defensible, but the category of timely or late performance depends on the actual prescribed period. The two assessments have different grounds.

Research criteria: establish the original command’s scope, the role of its time condition and any further evidence requiring make-up. Do not infer the final fiqh ruling solely from a general claim about what imperative wording entails.

title: What is a concession?
summary: Understand permitted latitude under an excuse while preserving the original requirement and the evidence governing the exception.
prerequisites: Know the difference between an original duty, permission, and make-up performance from lessons 2 and 8.

terms.definition: The wording used in §60 for the original requirement imposed by the Law; the lesson follows that passage’s terminology.
A concession: latitude granted because of an excuse or incapacity, with the original prohibiting cause remaining in the account given in §60.
An excuse relevant to the legal latitude under discussion; its effect must be established from the Law.
Omission or ellipsis; §58 discusses an understood condition omitted from the surface wording of the fasting verse.

basic.objective: Explain how a concession differs from treating the original requirement as simply absent in every circumstance.
explanation: Section 60 describes an original requirement and then a concession: latitude granted because of an excuse or incapacity while the prohibiting cause remains. Its example of otherwise forbidden food under necessity shows why an exceptional permission does not erase the general rule.

Sections 57–58 apply the problem to fasting during travel or illness. Ibn Rushd distinguishes interpretations of the relation between fasting now and fasting on other days. The classification depends on how the relevant address is understood. Calling something a concession therefore names a legal relationship that must be explained, rather than providing an answer by itself.

example.title: The traveller who fasts
example.text: Section 58 contrasts readings of the requirement to fast on other days. On the concession reading, the understood condition is that the traveller breaks the fast; travel alone does not by itself invalidate a fast performed during travel.

tasks: Why does §60’s exceptional permission not amount to unrestricted permission?
What omitted condition matters in §58’s account of the fasting verse?
feedback: The permission is connected to the excuse or necessity described. Its scope cannot be expanded merely by ignoring that condition or the continuing general prohibition.
The understood condition is that the person breaks the fast. The requirement of other days is then read in relation to that omitted condition, rather than attached to travel without qualification.

intermediate.objective: Distinguish the competing analyses of a traveller’s fast and connect the disagreement to interpretation.
explanation: Section 58 reports two alternatives to the concession analysis: the Ẓāhirī view that the fast performed then is invalid, and al-Karkhī’s view that the obligation concerns other days although earlier fasting is valid. These positions must remain separate. They agree in declining the particular ellipsis identified by Ibn Rushd, but do not draw the same conclusion about validity.

Sections 155 and 193–194 explain why understood import and omitted wording can carry different degrees of evidential force. The fasting dispute therefore connects Part I’s classification of the act with Part III’s methods of interpretation. The mere presence of an ellipsis does not show that every proposed supplement is justified.

example.title: One rejected supplement, two conclusions
example.text: In §58 al-Karkhī compares fasting in Ramaḍān with advancing alms before the year’s completion. The Ẓāhirī conclusion reported there instead denies validity. Their different results cannot be represented by a single ‘literal’ ruling.

tasks: What distinguishes al-Karkhī’s reported account from the Ẓāhirī account?
What must justify supplying an omitted condition in this reading?
feedback: Both locate the obligation on other days, but al-Karkhī allows the earlier fast to count, whereas the reported Ẓāhirī view denies its validity.

Contextual and legal evidence must support the understood meaning. The later language discussion supplies a method for assessing its strength; editorial insertion alone cannot establish the interpretation.

advanced.objective: Evaluate how the classification of a concession depends on interpretation, timing and the conditions of a particular case.
explanation: Section 57 compares the traveller’s and sick person’s duty with an extended-time obligation and questions the strict application of make-up terminology. Section 58 then reports competing interpretations, while §60 gives a central sense of concession and acknowledges other uses of the term. A rigorous account should test the fit between these examples rather than assume one definition resolves every case.

The final paragraph of §58 raises the case of illness involving feared death or severe harm and explicitly leaves its assessment to independent inquiry. Preserve that limitation. The passage does not authorize transferring an uncomplicated travel example to every medically serious circumstance.

example.title: The limit of a general classification
example.text: After explaining the concession reading, §58 raises a more difficult illness case. Its purpose is to mark a question still requiring judgement; it does not supply a completed ruling for every degree of illness.

tasks: How can the extended-time comparison illuminate the ordinary case without deciding every illness case?
Design a check of the omission argument using the Bidāya discussion located in B09.
feedback: The comparison explains alternative performance periods under the assumed conditions. Additional harm can change which conditions and evidence are relevant, so the analogy cannot be applied without further analysis.

Research criteria: compare the exact verse interpretation, reports used, distinct positions and scope of the cases. Record whether the applied discussion confirms, qualifies or complicates the theoretical formulation; do not claim a completed cross-text demonstration from the summary card alone.
